En casa los enchufes dan 230 V, pero las: At home the sockets give 230 V, but the towers crossing the countryside carry 400,000 V, so much that a spark would jump through the air if you came near. Why is the electricity not simply carried at 230 V?

<b>1841</b>James Prescott Joule mide que: 1841James Prescott Joule measures that the heat given off by a wire is proportional to the square of the current and to its resistance: the Joule effect.
<b>1882</b>Thomas Edison abre en Nueva Y: 1882Thomas Edison opens the first direct-current power station in New York. At 110 V, it cannot carry the light further than a mile.
<b>1886</b>William Stanley, con el trans: 1886William Stanley, with the Gaulard and Gibbs transformer, lights the town of Great Barrington with alternating current. The "war of the currents" between Edison and Westinghouse begins.
<b>1891</b>Una línea de 175 km lleva la: 1891A 175 km line carries electricity from Lauffen to the Frankfurt exhibition at 15,000 V, as three-phase alternating current. Alternating current wins the war.
La línea es un circuito en serie: la cen: The line is a series circuit: the power station as a voltage source, the two cables as two small resistors and the city as a large resistor that uses 10 MW. The power balance tells how much is lost in the cables.
Se abre con una fuente de 400 kV, dos ca: It opens with a 400 kV source, two 2.5 Ω cables and a 16 kΩ city. We get I = 25 A and about 1.56 kW in each cable. Try lowering the source to 20 kV and the city to 40 Ω.

La central está lejos de la ciudad, a 50: The power station is far from the city, 50 km away, and the city needs 10 MW, about 10,000 houses with everything switched on. The power that arrives along a line is $P = V I$: voltage times current.\n\nThe same power can be carried with high voltage and low current or with low voltage and high current. It seems the same, but it is not: cables are not perfect.
tiene cada cable de 50 km, y son dos: id: each 50 km cable has, and there are two: outward and return.
Cada cable es de aluminio, con 560 mm² d: Each cable is made of aluminium, with a cross-section of 560 mm²: $R = ρ L/S = 2.8·10^{−8} · 5·10^4/(5.6·10^{−4}) = ${m(RC, 1)} "Ω"$. For the outward and return, ${m(R, 0)} Ω.\n\nThe electrons collide with the atoms of the metal and heat it: this is the Joule effect, and the power lost is $P_p = I^2 R$. It goes with the square of the current: twice the current, four times the losses.

Si la línea fuera a 230 V, como los ench: If the line ran at 230 V, like the sockets, the current would be $I = P/V = 10^7/230 = ${m(datos.I230, 0)} "A"$.\n\nAnd the losses, $P_p = I^2 R = ${m(datos.I230, 0)}^2 · ${m(R, 0)} = ${m(datos.P230 / 1e9, 2)}·10^9 "W"$: far more than the power that was meant to be carried. In practice the cables would melt. That is why electricity does not travel at 230 V.

A 400 000 V, la corriente baja a $I = 10: At 400,000 V, the current drops to $I = 10^7/(4·10^5) = ${m(datos.I400k, 0)} "A"$, and the losses to $P_p = ${m(datos.I400k, 0)}^2 · ${m(R, 0)} = ${m(datos.P400k, 0)} "W"$. Multiplying the voltage by 1739 divides the losses by 1739², about three million.\n\nThat is why Spain's transmission lines run at 220 and 400 kV, with very tall towers and long insulators so the spark does not jump to the tower or the ground.
la tensión cambia en la proporción de la: the voltage changes in proportion to the turns of the coils.
Para subir y bajar la tensión se usa el: To raise and lower the voltage the transformer is used: two coils on the same iron core. The alternating current in the first creates a changing magnetic field that induces a voltage in the second (Faraday's law), in proportion to its turns: $V_2/V_1 = N_2/N_1$.\n\nPower is conserved (almost entirely), so if the voltage rises 20 times, the current falls 20 times: $V_1 I_1 = V_2 I_2$. It only works with alternating current: that is why the grid is alternating, at 50 Hz.
De la central al enchufe: From the power station to the socket
en varios saltos: transporte, distribuci: in several jumps: transmission, distribution and the neighbourhood transformer.
La central produce a unos 20 kV, un tran: The power station produces at about 20 kV, a transformer raises it to 400 kV for the long journey, at the entrance to the city it is lowered to 20 kV to distribute through the neighbourhoods and the transformer on the corner brings it down to 230 V for the houses.\n\nWith all that, the transmission network loses only around 1 or 2 % of the energy. For very long distances or cables under the sea, such as the one from the Peninsula to the Balearic Islands, high-voltage direct current is used, which today can be transformed with power electronics.
